papers.title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety lies at the core of developing and deploying large language models (LLMs). However, previous safety benchmarks only concern the safety in one language, e.g. the majority language in the pretraining data such as English. In this work, we build the first multilingual safety benchmark for LLMs, XSafety, in response to the global deployment of LLMs in practice. XSafety covers 14 kinds of commonly used safety issues across 10 languages that span several language families. We utilize XSafety to empirically study the multilingual safety for 4 widely-used LLMs, including both close-API and open-source models. Experimental results show that all LLMs produce significantly more unsafe responses for non-English queries than English ones, indicating the necessity of developing safety alignment for non-English languages. In addition, we propose several simple and effective prompting methods to improve the multilingual safety of ChatGPT by evoking safety knowledge and improving cross-lingual generalization of safety alignment. Our prompting method can significantly reduce the ratio of unsafe responses from 19.1% to 9.7% for non-English queries. We release our data at https://github.com/Jarviswang94/Multilingual_safety_benchmark.

papers.title: Safety Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models
papers.abstract: With the rapid popularity of large language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, a growing amount of attention is paid to their safety concerns. These models may generate insulting and discriminatory content, reflect incorrect social values, and may be used for malicious purposes such as fraud and dissemination of misleading information. Evaluating and enhancing their safety is particularly essential for the wide application of large language models (LLMs). To further promote the safe deployment of LLMs, we develop a Chinese LLM safety assessment benchmark. Our benchmark explores the comprehensive safety performance of LLMs from two perspectives: 8 kinds of typical safety scenarios and 6 types of more challenging instruction attacks. Our benchmark is based on a straightforward process in which it provides the test prompts and evaluates the safety of the generated responses from the evaluated model. In evaluation, we utilize the LLM's strong evaluation ability and develop it as a safety evaluator by prompting. On top of this benchmark, we conduct safety assessments and analyze 15 LLMs including the OpenAI GPT series and other well-known Chinese LLMs, where we observe some interesting findings. For example, we find that instruction attacks are more likely to expose safety issues of all LLMs. Moreover, to promote the development and deployment of safe, responsible, and ethical AI, we publicly release SafetyPrompts including 100k augmented prompts and responses by LLMs.

papers.title: Safety at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey of Large Model and Agent Safety
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large models, driven by their exceptional abilities in learning and generalization through large-scale pre-training, has reshaped the landscape of Artificial Intelligence (AI). These models are now foundational to a wide range of applications, including conversational AI, recommendation systems, autonomous driving, content generation, medical diagnostics, and scientific discovery. However, their widespread deployment also exposes them to significant safety risks, raising concerns about robustness, reliability, and ethical implications. This survey provides a systematic review of current safety research on large models, covering Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and large-model-powered Agents. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We present a comprehensive taxonomy of safety threats to these models, including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, backdoor attacks, jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, energy-latency attacks, data and model extraction attacks, and emerging agent-specific threats. (2) We review defense strategies proposed for each type of attacks if available and summarize the commonly used datasets and benchmarks for safety research. (3) Building on this, we identify and discuss the open challenges in large model safety, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety evaluations, scalable and effective defense mechanisms, and sustainable data practices. More importantly, we highlight the necessity of collective efforts from the research community and international collaboration. Our work can serve as a useful reference for researchers and practitioners, fostering the ongoing development of comprehensive defense systems and platforms to safeguard AI models.

papers.title: Enhanced Diagnostic and Interpretable Model for Febrile Diseases Using Explainable AI and Large Language Model
papers.abstract: <p><span>Tropical febrile diseases pose significant public health challenges in tropical regions, particularly in resource-limited settings, where timely and accurate diagnoses are critical for effective disease management. However, existing diagnostic systems are black-box and often lack interpretability, making it difficult for healthcare practitioners to understand and trust machine learning (ML) predictions. Additionally, the existing system excludes younger patients, limiting its applicability. This study aimed to develop an integrated diagnostic system that enhances interpretability by leveraging machine learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), and a large language model (LLM). A dataset comprising 3,914 patient records with 32 symptoms was obtained from a New Frontiers in Research Fund-sponsored project and preprocessed for analysis. Random Forest (RF) was trained with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation to optimize its performance. The tuned model achieved high diagnostic performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in diagnosing six febrile diseases. To enhance interpretability, a Model Interpretability Framework (MIF) was incorporated, integrating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) for visual insights and ChatGPT for textual explanations. This combination provided users with a clear understanding of the diagnostic process, addressing the limitations of black-box ML models. The system was implemented using Python in a development environment that included Google Colaboratory, Visual Studio Code, Flet, and MySQL for database management. Agile development methodology and Unified Modeling Language tools were employed to create a user-friendly design for clinicians and patients. The diagnostic system was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics. The RF model achieved outstanding precision for most diseases, high recall (≥0.97), and an AUC-ROC of 0.99, indicating nearly flawless training performance with few misclassifications. On the test dataset, the model performed better in diagnosing malaria (F1-score = 88%, precision = 85%), urinary tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 80%), and respiratory tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 77%). The evaluated system demonstrated strong predictive performance, correctly identifying 72 out of 99 tested patient cases, with 26 cases misclassified and one case completely missed. It achieved the highest detection rates for Malaria and HIV/AIDS, accurately identifying all cases without false positives. This work enhances diagnostic solutions for tropical healthcare settings by improving explainability and ensuring inclusivity for younger patients, addressing key limitations in existing systems. The integration of ML, XAI, and LLM enhances diagnostic performance and lays the groundwork for future AI-driven healthcare innovations, ultimately improving health outcomes in resource-scarce regions. Healthcare providers should adopt this system to enhance the efficiency of disease diagnosis and extend the system to diagnose additional medical conditions.&nbsp;</span></p>

literature_themes.theme: Safety Assessment of Large Language Models Across Languages
literature_themes.summary: This cluster of papers focuses on the safety concerns associated with large language models (LLMs) in multilingual contexts. It introduces benchmarks for assessing safety in both English and non-English languages, highlighting the increased risks for non-English queries. The studies propose methods to improve safety alignment and evaluate the safety performance of various LLMs, including those specifically designed for Chinese. A comprehensive survey also reviews safety threats and defense strategies for large models.
literature_themes.limitations: The studies primarily focus on specific languages and may not cover all languages or dialects comprehensively. There is also a need for more extensive testing across diverse cultural contexts to fully understand the implications of LLM safety. Additionally, the effectiveness of proposed safety improvements may vary based on the model architecture and training data.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster identifies a significant research gap in the safety assessment of LLMs across multiple languages, emphasizing the necessity for multilingual safety benchmarks and methodologies. It supports the need for further exploration into safety enhancements and the ethical implications of deploying LLMs in diverse linguistic and cultural settings.

summary: The retrieved literature highlights significant safety concerns in large language models (LLMs), particularly in multilingual contexts, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety assessments and benchmarks across diverse languages. Studies reveal that non-English queries often yield more unsafe responses, necessitating improved prompting strategies. Additionally, the integration of LLMs into few-shot recommender systems shows promise for enhancing representation capabilities, though empirical validation remains limited. Overall, there is a critical gap in understanding the interpretability and effectiveness of LLMs in various applications, underscoring the importance of safety and controllability in their deployment.
scholarly_positioning: Prior research has extensively documented safety concerns in large language models (LLMs), particularly in multilingual contexts, yet these studies often focus narrowly on specific languages or models, leaving a significant gap in comprehensive safety assessments across diverse linguistic and cultural settings. The existing methodologies lack interpretability and fail to address the complexities introduced by integrating LLMs into practical applications, such as recommender systems. Furthermore, while some studies propose safety benchmarks, they do not sufficiently explore the implications of these safety measures on model controllability and user trust. This proposed research aims to bridge these gaps by developing interpretable internal representations that enhance both safety and controllability in LLMs, contributing to a broader discourse on ethical AI deployment and the necessity for robust, multilingual safety frameworks.

research_scope: This study will investigate the safety and controllability of large language models (LLMs) in the context of multilingual recommender systems, focusing on the integration of interpretable internal representations. The target population will consist of users interacting with LLM-enhanced recommendation systems across English and Chinese languages. The evaluation period will span six months, during which the models will be assessed using a benchmark that includes safety metrics and user trust calibration measures. A control group will utilize traditional recommendation algorithms without LLM integration. Primary outcomes will include the frequency of unsafe responses and user trust levels, while secondary outcomes will assess the effectiveness of interpretability methods in enhancing user understanding and satisfaction with recommendations.
concept_definition: The study focuses on large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-3 and BERT, which are assessed for their internal representations, specifically hidden states and internal activations that are accessible during evaluation. Internal representations refer to the model's learned features that capture semantic and contextual information. Interpretability methods employed include probing (analyzing model behavior), attribution (identifying input contributions), attention visualization (showing focus areas), and safety monitors (detecting unsafe outputs). Explanations generated are aimed at users interacting with LLM-enhanced recommendation systems. Safety outcomes are defined as the rate of unsafe responses (harmful outputs), over-refusal (excessive refusal to answer), jailbreak success (bypassing safety measures), harmful compliance (following harmful prompts), and precision/recall of refusals. User trust is operationalized through trust calibration (alignment of user expectations with model performance), blind trust (unquestioning reliance), perceived transparency (user understanding of model workings), and appropriate reliance (correctly trusting the model's outputs). Controllability refers to the ability to guide model behavior in desired directions, alignment ensures model objectives are consistent with user values, and fairness addresses equitable treatment across diverse user groups.
technical_feasibility: The study requires open-source model access or hidden state extraction to analyze internal representations. If only API models are available, the design should shift towards output-level explanation or black-box evaluation. Additionally, it necessitates labeled datasets for multilingual annotation, native-speaker validation for cultural context, human participants for trust calibration measures, ethics approval for user studies, GPU resources for model training and evaluation, and established annotation protocols for consistency. A feasible adjustment would be to focus on available open-source models or adapt the evaluation to rely more on user interaction with outputs rather than internal states.
gap: There is a need for comprehensive multilingual safety assessments of large language models (LLMs) that include diverse cultural contexts and languages beyond English and Chinese, focusing on interpretability and user trust.
question: How do interpretable internal representations in large language models enhance user trust and reduce unsafe responses in multilingual recommender systems compared to traditional recommendation algorithms?
theoretical_mechanism: The proposed research posits that interpretable internal representations (independent variable) in large language models (LLMs) enhance user trust (dependent variable) through perceived transparency (mediator). This transparency allows users to better understand model outputs, which can lead to increased satisfaction and reliance on the system. Concurrently, the integration of safety detection mechanisms and filters (mediators) reduces the rate of unsafe responses (system-level outcome) by steering model behavior towards safer outputs. The effectiveness of these mechanisms may be moderated by the cultural context of the user, impacting both system-level outcomes (e.g., refusal accuracy, jailbreak success) and user-level outcomes (e.g., trust calibration). The theoretical framework draws on concepts from human-computer interaction and safety in AI, suggesting a causal chain where improved internal representation leads to enhanced safety and user trust. Assumptions requiring empirical validation include the effectiveness of interpretability methods in diverse cultural contexts and the direct influence of user understanding on their trust and reliance on LLM outputs.
hypothesis: Interpretable internal representations in large language models will significantly reduce the frequency of unsafe responses in multilingual recommender systems compared to traditional recommendation algorithms, thereby enhancing user trust.

proposal: This research proposal aims to investigate the role of interpretable internal representations in large language models (LLMs) to enhance safety and controllability within multilingual recommender systems, specifically focusing on English and Chinese contexts. Internal representations refer to the model's learned features that capture semantic and contextual information, while interpretability methods include probing, attribution, and attention visualization. The study addresses the critical gap in comprehensive multilingual safety assessments, particularly the lack of interpretability and user trust in LLM applications, as existing literature highlights significant safety concerns but often focuses narrowly on specific languages or models, leaving a gap in understanding the implications of these concerns across diverse cultural contexts. The central research question is: How do interpretable internal representations in LLMs enhance user trust and reduce unsafe responses in multilingual recommender systems compared to traditional recommendation algorithms? The theoretical mechanism posits that improved internal representations (independent variable) enhance perceived transparency (mediator), leading to increased user trust (dependent variable) and reduced unsafe responses (system-level outcome) through safety detection mechanisms (mediator). The falsifiable hypothesis states that interpretable internal representations in LLMs will significantly reduce unsafe responses in multilingual recommender systems compared to traditional algorithms, thereby enhancing user trust. Constructs will be operationalized through measurements such as probing accuracy and unsafe response rates at the model level, while user trust will be assessed through trust calibration surveys and behavioral logs. The methodology includes developing a multilingual safety benchmark (XSafety) that evaluates LLMs across multiple languages, focusing on unsafe response rates and user trust calibration, and conducting user studies with appropriate controls, such as traditional recommendation algorithms defined by standard collaborative filtering techniques. Expected contributions include a theoretical framework linking interpretability to user trust, a novel multilingual safety benchmark, and empirical findings on interpretability's effectiveness in enhancing user understanding, while acknowledging limitations such as potential cultural context misalignment and user engagement issues, which will be mitigated through native speaker validation and incentivized participation.

Next band requirements: To enhance novelty, the proposal should articulate a clearer theoretical or methodological innovation that significantly advances the field.

Major weaknesses: There is insufficient detail on the experimental controls and the robustness of the evaluation metrics. The proposal does not adequately address potential confounds. Next band requirements: Providing a more detailed experimental design that includes controls for confounding variables and a clearer justification for evaluation metrics would enhance feasibility.
